passages.quote:
Before you dismiss an employee

Dismissal is when an employer ends an employee’s contract.

You must have a valid reason for dismissing an employee and act reasonably when making your decision.

Your company should have its own disciplinary, capability, sickness absence and dismissal policies. If not follow the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service (Acas) Code of Practice on disciplinary and grievance procedures.

This Code of Practice is the minimum an employer should follow for handling these issues.

Fair reasons for dismissal

You may be able to dismiss an employee fairly because of:

conduct, such as misconduct or gross misconduct

capability, if they cannot do the job to the required standard, long-term ill health or do not have the necessary qualifications

redundancy, if their job is no longer needed

a legal restriction, if continuing to employ them in the role would break the law, for example if a driver loses the licence they need for their job

some other substantial reason, for example a fixed-term contract ending, a client refusing to work with the employee or the employee refusing reasonable changes to their terms and conditions

You must follow the appropriate procedure for the reason you are considering dismissal. For example, if an employee’s role is no longer needed, you must follow a redundancy process.

If an employee has a long-term illness or disability, dismissal should be a last resort. For example, you should first consider how you can support them to return to work or you may also need to make reasonable adjustments if they are disabled.

Follow a fair procedure

The procedure you need to follow will depend on the reason for dismissal. In most cases, you should:

investigate the facts

tell the employee about the problem and that dismissal is a possible outcome

give the employee a reasonable opportunity to respond

consider alternatives to dismissal

make a reasonable and consistent decision based on the evidence

tell the employee your decision, why you have made it, when their employment will end and what notice they will receive

give the employee the opportunity to appeal

Keep a written record of the process and decision.

Keep information about the employee and their dismissal confidential.

Gross misconduct

Gross misconduct is conduct that is very serious or has very serious effects. Examples include:

fraud

physical violence

gross negligence

serious insubordination

You may be able to dismiss an employee for gross misconduct without notice or notice pay. You must still investigate and follow a fair procedure.

You must still pay the employee any money they are entitled to, including:

wages for work they have already done

accrued holiday pay

expenses you owe them

Other payments or benefits may also be due depending on their contract.
